title: Settings in a design critique tool
excerpt: Settings for a critique tool should cover who is on the review, what the client link opens, and what resolve does. Pin colors and billing can wait on a lower shelf.
alt: An OPEN sign hanging in a shop window, with the word SHOP printed on the glass, a simple label for who is allowed in.
caption: The sign says what the room is for. Photograph via Unsplash.

faqs.question: What belongs on the first critique settings screen?
faqs.answer: Who can comment or resolve, the client link's power and expiry, which events send mail, what resolve does to a note, and which version reviewers land on. Personal mute belongs in a separate group from file settings, so it never sits next to delete.

faqs.question: How should resolve be configured?
faqs.answer: Pick one behavior and write it in a sentence, with a preview of the pin. Resolved notes can stay dim on the frame or move to a list. Do not offer three toggles that overlap. A temporary hide during a meeting is a view, not a change to the file for everyone.

faqs.question: What should a client link stay pinned to?
faqs.answer: The version the owner chose, even if a newer sketch is uploaded into the same file. Say that in the cabinet. Exporting a review should state whether internal notes are included, and the default should leave them out.

markdown:
Keep design critique tool settings ux as a cabinet, not a second product. Group what a small team leaving comments on a screen changes often: who is on the review, how they are notified, and what "resolved" means. Bury the rest.

The W3C's WCAG overview holds interfaces to perceivable, operable, understandable, and robust principles. A setting qualifies when the label says what will change on the frame, the control can be used without a manual, and the same word means the same thing in the cabinet and on the note.

## The frequent shelf

A small team revisits only a few decisions. Put those on the first settings screen.

- Who is on this review, and whether they can comment, resolve, or only view.
- Whether a client link exists, what it allows, and when it ends.
- Which events send mail: a mention, a new version, an approval asked of you.
- What resolve does: dim the note, hide it, or keep it in a list.
- The default version reviewers land on.

Theme, a library of stamp icons, and a workspace name can live lower. They do not change the critique. A cabinet that opens on appearance has mistaken the costume for the work. The frame is the product. Settings only keep the frame trustworthy.

Labels should sound like the team. "Who can comment," not "ACL." "Mail me when someone asks for me," not "Notification matrix." A founder looking for the client link should find it by reading headings, not by remembering your information architecture. If a heading needs a tooltip, rewrite the heading.

Split file settings from personal ones. Who is invited, and what the client link does, belong to the file. Whether you receive mail, and how you like the canvas to fit the window, belong to the person. Mixing them puts a personal mute button next to "delete the review." Those are not neighbors.

## Resolve, versions, and the landing default

Resolve is a setting because teams disagree about it, and the disagreement should be chosen once. Some want resolved notes to stay as dim pins, so the history of the frame is visible. Some want them in a list, off the canvas, so the meeting stays on what is open. Pick a default, write it in a sentence, and show a tiny preview of a pin in each state. "Resolved notes stay on the frame, dimmed." The preview prevents a settings argument that is really a vocabulary argument.

Do not offer three overlapping toggles: hide resolved, archive resolved, collapse resolved. One behavior. If a person wants a temporary hide during a meeting, that can be a view control on the canvas, not a setting that changes the file for everyone. Say the difference. "This hides notes for you, in this meeting. It does not resolve them."

The landing version is a company-or-file default with a sharp edge. "Open the latest version" is right when the latest is the one under review. It is wrong when someone uploaded a sketch into the same file and pulled the client's link onto it. Let the owner pin the version the link opens, and say that pin in the cabinet. "The client link opens Thursday's draft, even if you upload a newer one." That sentence prevents an accidental premiere.

Replacing or deleting a version belongs here only if it is dangerous, and it is. Require the version's name in the confirmation. "Delete 'after legal.' 14 notes stay in the archive and leave the canvas." If deletion destroys notes, say that louder and offer archive instead. A small team can lose an afternoon of critique to a tidy impulse. The cabinet should make tidy slightly harder than leaving things alone.

## Notifications without a mail storm

Default to the few mails a small team will still read. A mention. A new version on a file you are reviewing. An ask to approve, if you use approval. Do not default to mail on every comment, every view, and every resolve. People mute the product, and then they miss the mention. Quiet is the accessible default, in the ordinary sense and in the WCAG sense that the interface should be understandable rather than noisy.

Let each person turn mentions off for themselves without turning them off for the file. Show the company default and the personal override as two rows, so a lead can tell which one they are editing. "The review mails mentions. You have paused your own mail until Monday." That second sentence belongs in the cabinet and, briefly, on the file, so they remember why Sam did not reply.

A new version can mail the reviewers with the version's name and the uploader's sentence, if they wrote one. The setting is whether that mail exists, and the field for the sentence can sit on the upload as well as here. Do not make them come to settings to write "legal asked us to shorten the hero." That sentence belongs to the version. The cabinet only decides whether it gets sent.

Digests, if you offer one, should list unresolved notes in the note's own words, with the file name. A digest that says "23 events" is a setting you can bury, or skip. Volume is not the object. The open note is.

## Client links and required voices

The client link is a frequent and dangerous setting, so it stays on the shelf even though it is also a permission. Show the URL, the power it grants, the version it opens, and the expiry, in one group, with a preview line the client would see. "You can comment until Friday." If you change the power, say what happens to comments already left. They remain. The link's future changes. Do not rewrite history because the toggle moved.

Required approvers, if you use them, are a setting on the review, not a workflow product. "Sam has to approve before this is marked done." One sentence, one person or a small set, and a way to see that the file is still waiting. A builder of branching approval chains is a second product. A small team will not maintain it. They will work around it in chat, which is the failure you are trying to avoid.

Who may change these settings should be written on them. A commenter opening the cabinet should see the client link's status and not an editable expiry that errors on save. Disabled with a reason, for anything they would look for. Hidden, for stamp packs and billing. "Only Riley can change the client link." The name is better than the word owner, because small teams think in names.

## Stamps, exports, and the things that can wait

A set of stamp icons, a custom cursor, and a choice of pin colors feel like settings and behave like a toy. If you offer them, put them below the shelf, default them to one pin style the whole team shares, and do not let a personal color change the meaning of a note. Red for "blocking" is a status, and it belongs next to resolve, with a word, not as a favorite color. WCAG's perceivable principle is the practical test: meaning that exists only as a hue will fail in a meeting and fail for some reviewers entirely. The word has to travel with the color.

Exporting a review to a PDF or a deck is a rare action with a real consequence, because the export is a copy that will go stale. Put it low in the cabinet. Say what it includes. "Friday's draft, unresolved notes, no internal comments." Let the owner see the internal comments excluded before they send it to a client. A default export that includes everything is how a frank note leaves the building. The confirmation can be the same sentence the client link already uses, so you do not maintain two voices for the same boundary.

Workspace name, billing, and the logo on a shared link matter, and they are not weekly. They can sit on an account page the owner finds from the cabinet's footer. The file's shelf should not open there. A teammate who came to fix notifications should not walk through an invoice to do it.

## Review the shelf with one real file

Change the resolve behavior and confirm the canvas matches the sentence. Pin a client link to an older version, upload a newer one, and confirm the link did not follow. Mute yourself and confirm you still see mentions on the frame. Delete nothing in the test if you can avoid it. If you must, use a copy, and read the confirmation out loud before you press it.

If a frequent change was hard to find, move it up. If a rare change sat next to "who can comment," move it down and add the consequence. The cabinet is finished when a teammate can predict what the frame, the mail, and the client will do after a save.

The next room is no longer a critique. A member community has its own first screen, and its own object. [The first screen of a member community](/blog/the-first-screen-of-a-member-community) asks what that object is, and which single action the member should see before any tour of the club.

Hanabi designs this kind of cabinet in Figma next to the frame it affects, then builds it in Next.js, React, and TypeScript so the sentence in settings and the sentence on the file cannot drift. Prisma and PostgreSQL hold the seat, the expiry, and the resolve rule. Tailwind keeps the shelf visually quiet. Motion can confirm a save. It should not introduce the settings.

If your critique settings have become a product of their own, see [Hanabi's services](https://tryhanabi.com/#services). Bring the few decisions your team actually revisits. Those belong on the shelf. The rest can wait.
